prompt: how do i learn my spelling words for friday
reply:
Say the word out loud first ✏️. Then cover it and write it. Peek and check every letter 👀.

[POEM]Look at the word and say it slow,
cover it up and off you go,
write it down then take a peek,
spelling gets stronger every week.[/POEM]

[CHIPS]Try one word now|Use it in sentences|Which word is hardest[/CHIPS]

prompt: i keep forgetting my homework notebook at school
reply:
This happens to lots of children 🎒. Pack your bag before you leave class. Put the homework book on top ✅.

[BIG]📓[/BIG]

[CHIPS]Pack before you play|Make a bag list|Ask a class buddy[/CHIPS]

prompt: teacher talks and i forget to write it down
reply:
Your hand cannot race your ears 👂. Write only the big words. Fill the gaps at home ✏️.

[CHIPS]What counts as big|Leave a gap|Ask a friend after[/CHIPS]

prompt: what do i do first when i get home from school
reply:
Eat something and rest a little 🍎. Then homework, before you get sleepy. Play is the reward after 🛼.

[STEPS]snack and rest|homework next|then play[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Try it today|What if too tired|Pick a homework time[/CHIPS]

prompt: i was sick and missed school yesterday
reply:
Welcome back 🌼. Ask a friend which pages the class did. Copy one page today, not everything.

[BIG]📖[/BIG]

[CHIPS]Ask a friend today|Tell teacher I missed[/CHIPS]

prompt: my pencil box is a big mess
reply:
Tip everything out on the table. Keep what you use every day. The rest can stay home 🏠.

[BIG]🖍️[/BIG]

[CHIPS]Two pencils one eraser|Sort it today|Check it every friday[/CHIPS]

prompt: teacher gave homework but i forgot what to do
reply:
First look in your homework diary 📔. If it is not there, ask a friend. Asking is always allowed ✋.

[CHIPS]Check the diary|Ask a friend|Tell teacher tomorrow[/CHIPS]

prompt: my teacher put a red cross on three sums
reply:
A red cross just shows where to look. Try those three again, slowly. Not right yet means nearly right 💪.

[BIG]🔍[/BIG]

[CHIPS]Redo one sum|Find the small slip|Show teacher tomorrow[/CHIPS]

prompt: i have to show my project to the class what do i say first
reply:
Start with what you made 🎨. Then one thing you liked doing. Then say thank you 👏.

[STEPS]say what you made|say your favourite bit|say thank you[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Practise with amma|Say it once now|Hold it up high[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is a dictionary for
reply:
It is a big word helper 📖. It tells you what words mean. It shows how to spell them 🔤.

[QUIZ]In a dictionary, which comes first: ant or bee?[/QUIZ]

[CHIPS]Bee comes first|Ant comes first|Both together[/CHIPS]

prompt: where is a good place to do my homework
reply:
Pick one spot and keep it 🪑. A table with light and no TV. Your brain learns: this means work 🧠.

[STEPS]pick your spot|clear the table|keep water nearby[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Pick my spot now|Clear the table|Show amma my spot[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i know if my homework is finished properly
reply: Read it slowly one more time 👀. Check every question has an answer. Now read your last line aloud ✍️.

prompt: why do we have to do homework
reply:
Footballers practise the same kick many times ⚽. Homework is your practice. Your brain grows when it tries alone.

[BIG]💪[/BIG]

[CHIPS]Start with one sum|Set a small timer|What if it's hard[/CHIPS]

prompt: what should i actually write down in my notes during class
reply:
Notes are not a photocopy of the lesson — they are your shortlist 📝. Write whatever the teacher repeats, whatever goes on the board, and any worked example. Leave a wide margin so future-you can add questions 🙋.

[CHIPS]Try the wide margin|What can I skip|Show a note layout[/CHIPS]

prompt: my notes are so long i cannot revise from them
reply:
Long notes usually mean you copied; short notes mean you understood ✂️. Take one page and squeeze it onto a single card. If a line will not fit, ask whether it was ever the main idea 🃏.

[STEPS]one heading|three key points|one example[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Squeeze one page now|Pick the key points|Try a mind map[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i make flashcards that actually work
reply:
A flashcard does its real work in the pause 🔄. One idea per card, question on one side, answer on the other — and always guess out loud before you flip 🃏.

[STEPS]guess out loud|flip and check|wrong ones go again[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Make five cards now|Cards for maths|Paper or app[/CHIPS]

prompt: i have a test on friday and five chapters to cover where do i start
reply:
Which chapter would you least like to see on the paper? Start there, while your energy is fresh 😬. Give the scary chapters your long slots, and save the last evening for a quick loop through all five ✅.

[CHIPS]Rank the five chapters|Plan monday to thursday|How to test myself[/CHIPS]

prompt: our teacher said read chapter 6 before class how do i do that properly
reply: Pre-reading is not really reading — it is scouting 🗺️. Skim every heading, look at the pictures and captions, then read the end-of-chapter summary first, so the lesson has somewhere to land 👀. Give chapter 6 three minutes of scouting right now, before you read a single paragraph.

prompt: how do i find a word in the dictionary fast
reply:
Use the two guide words at the top of each page 📖 — they are the first and last entry on it. If your word sits alphabetically between them, it is on that page; if not, flip on 🔍.

[QUIZ]Guide words are lamp and later. Is last on that page?[/QUIZ]

[CHIPS]No, an earlier page|No, a later page|Yes, it is between[/CHIPS]

prompt: the dictionary gave four meanings how do i pick the right one
reply:
Let your sentence choose 🧐. Check the little label first — n for noun, v for verb — then read each meaning back into your own sentence. The one that does not sound silly is the one you want ✅.

[STEPS]check the word label|read each meaning|pick what fits[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Try it with bank|What does adj mean[/CHIPS]

prompt: i always spell receive wrong
reply:
Receive obeys the old rhyme: i before e, except after c 🔤. There is a c right before, so it goes c-e-i-v-e. The rhyme leaks though — science and their both break it — so keep it for c words 💡.

[FACT]Almost every English word with a q has a u right after.[/FACT]

[CHIPS]Test me on ceiling|Words that break it|Try look-cover-write[/CHIPS]

prompt: i copied my friend's notes but i still do not understand the lesson
reply:
Copying moves ink, not ideas ✍️. Find the one line where you get lost, turn it into a question, and hunt for it in the textbook — books usually explain what a friend's shorthand skipped. If it still will not budge, that question is exactly what you take to your teacher 🙋.

[CHIPS]Write the question down|Find it in textbook|Ask teacher tomorrow[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i make my presentation slides not boring
reply:
Slides are posters, not scripts 🖼️. One idea per slide, very few words, and a picture that does the explaining while you say the rest out loud. If the whole talk is readable on screen, people read ahead and stop listening 🎤.

[STEPS]one idea per slide|few words|one strong picture[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Practise saying it aloud|Pick better pictures|What about endings[/CHIPS]

prompt: i got 11 out of 25 in my maths test what should i do now
reply:
Fourteen marks are sitting there waiting to be collected 🔎. Sort every wrong answer into two piles — did not know it, and knew it but slipped. Those piles need completely different fixes, so the sorting is the useful part 💪.

[CHIPS]Sort the wrong ones|Redo two questions|Fix a careless slip[/CHIPS]

prompt: should i do the easy homework first or the hard one first
reply:
Both work, so choose on purpose 🤔. Easy first gets you moving and shortens the list; hard first spends your freshest thinking where it counts. A good middle: start the hard one, and keep an easy task as your finish line 🏁.

[CHIPS]Try hard first today|Try easy first today|How long per task[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i stop making careless mistakes in tests
reply:
Careless slips are rarely random — they tend to repeat in a small set ✏️. Collect yours for a week: copied a number wrong, dropped a minus sign, answered a different question. Then check only for those at the end, instead of re-reading everything 🕵️.

[STEPS]list your usual slips|save the last minutes|check only those[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Start my slip list|Try it in homework|Which slips are common[/CHIPS]

prompt: is there a note taking system worth learning or is it all hype
reply:
Most systems are the same trick in different clothes: force yourself to process, not transcribe. The cheapest is the two-column layout, often called Cornell — notes on the right, questions you write yourself on the left, a two-line summary at the bottom. The summary is the part that works, because you cannot fake it 📝. Try it on one lesson before converting your whole notebook.

[CHIPS]Try one lesson|What goes on left|Does it suit maths[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i revise a subject i find completely boring
reply:
Boring often means no hooks yet — nothing in the topic connects to anything you already care about. Two things shift it: turn the syllabus into questions you would genuinely want answered, and work in short blocks with a hard stop, so it never becomes an endless afternoon. And stop re-reading; make the material argue back by testing yourself on it 🎯.

[CHIPS]Turn topics into questions|Set a hard stop|Try a self-test[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is the best way to use past papers
reply:
Not as reading material — that is the usual mistake. Sit one properly: timer on, phone in another room, no notes, then mark it against the scheme without being kind to yourself. The marking is where the learning is, especially the marks lost to misread instructions rather than to missing knowledge 📄.

[STEPS]sit it timed|mark it honestly|log what cost marks[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Do one timed paper|How to mark it|What to log[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i split a two hour revision session so it is not wasted
reply:
Two unbroken hours is mostly an illusion — attention fades long before the clock does. Split it into blocks with a real break between, and open each block by writing down what you remember from the last one. Finish by closing the book and listing three things unprompted; whatever you cannot list is tomorrow's starting point ⏳.

[CHIPS]Plan tonight's blocks|Try the recall list[/CHIPS]

prompt: how should i split my time in a three hour exam paper
reply:
Think in marks, not questions. A hundred-mark paper over a hundred and eighty minutes leaves a bit under two minutes per mark, and it is worth keeping ten of those minutes back for reading at the start and checking at the end ⏱️. When a question runs past its budget, leave a gap and move on — a fresh question pays better than a stuck one.

[STEPS]read the paper first|budget by marks|leave gaps to revisit[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Work out my budget|When to move on[/CHIPS]

prompt: i have three assignments due in the same week
reply:
Give each one two numbers: hours it will honestly take, and marks it carries. Start where a little effort buys the most marks, and give the low-value one a deliberate ceiling rather than quietly abandoning it. Book the blocks into a real calendar too — a to-do list hides how little time is left 🗓️.

[STEPS]list hours and marks|rank by best value|book the blocks[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Rank them by marks|Set a time ceiling|Block out this week[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i take notes from a long recorded lecture
reply:
How often have you rewound a video and still written nothing? The pause button can quietly make you lazier, because rewinding always feels available. Try one pass at normal speed, noting only headings and whatever gets stressed, and leaving gaps where you lost the thread — then rewatch only the gaps ⏯️.

[CHIPS]Try the gap method|Notes for maths videos|How to rewatch[/CHIPS]

prompt: why bother with a thesaurus if i already know the word
reply:
Because near-synonyms are not equal. Thrifty, careful and stingy all describe spending little, but only one of them is an insult 🧠. A thesaurus is for choosing precisely, not for sounding clever — a fancy word you have never met in a real sentence is how writing starts sounding odd. Check any new word in a dictionary before it goes in.

[FACT]Thesaurus comes from a Greek word meaning treasure store.[/FACT]

[CHIPS]Try three word swaps|Check one in dictionary|When to stay simple[/CHIPS]

prompt: i have to learn about a hundred biology terms this term
reply:
A hundred separate facts is unlearnable; a hundred connected ones is not. Group them by the system they belong to, then attack the word parts — once cardio means heart and itis means inflammation, whole clusters decode themselves. For the leftovers that follow no logic, spaced flashcards are honest work 🧬.

[FACT]Mnemonic and Mnemosyne, the Greek goddess of memory, share one root word.[/FACT]

[CHIPS]Group by body system|Learn common word parts|Start with ten terms[/CHIPS]

prompt: i asked my teacher and i still did not get her explanation
reply:
Then say exactly that — respectfully, it is one of the most useful sentences in a classroom. 'I followed you until the third step, then I lost it' tells a teacher where to restart; 'I don't understand' gives them nothing to work with. If the bell is about to go, ask for the name of the topic so you can read it up, and come back after class 🙋.

[CHIPS]Find my stuck point|Practise the sentence|Who else can help[/CHIPS]

prompt: i got my paper back covered in red and i just filed it away
reply:
Understandable — and probably the most expensive habit in school. A marked paper is a free map of what to fix, and it goes stale fast, because you still remember what you were thinking when you wrote it. Give it twenty minutes: rewrite two wrong answers properly, and note beside each whether it was knowledge, method, or a slip 🗂️.

[STEPS]pick two wrong answers|rewrite them properly|label the cause[/STEPS]

[CHIPS]Redo two answers|Start an error log|Sort the mistakes[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i prepare for a presentation where the class can ask questions
reply:
Prepare the questions, not only the talk. Write the five things you would ask if you were half-listening in the back row, and answer each in a line — most real questions turn out to be versions of those. Rehearse saying 'I don't know, I'll find out' out loud, because using it once, calmly, beats bluffing 🎤.

[CHIPS]List likely questions|Practise the honest answer[/CHIPS]

prompt: i missed a week of school for a family wedding how do i catch up
reply:
Do not try to reconstruct the week — triage it. Get the list of topics covered, mark the ones the next lessons build on, and do those first; the rest can be filled in over the fortnight. Borrow notes by all means, but read them the same day, while whoever wrote them is still around to decode them 📚.

[CHIPS]Get the topic list|Which topics come first|Ask a friend today[/CHIPS]

prompt: is making a revision timetable actually useful or just procrastination
reply:
It turns into procrastination the moment it gets colourful 🎨. A useful one takes ten minutes, names topics rather than subjects, and leaves about a third of the week empty for the days that go wrong. Judge it at the end of the week: if you did not follow it, the plan was too optimistic, and that is information rather than a verdict on you.

[QUIZ]Which revision hour usually earns more: re-reading, or answering from memory?[/QUIZ]

[CHIPS]Answering from memory|Re-reading the chapter|Both the same[/CHIPS]
